content: Calcium supplements should be administered only in cases of hyperkalemia with significant electrocardiographic (ECG) abnormalities. Calcium works by stabilizing the cardiac membranes, thereby counteracting the effects of elevated potassium levels. The recommended dose is 5 to 10 mL of a 10% calcium solution (equivalent to 0.5 to 1 gram of calcium) administered via intravenous infusion over 2 to 3 minutes. Central venous access is preferred for this administration. Alternatively, calcium gluconate can be given at a dose of 1 gram (10 mL of a 10% solution) infused slowly. This can be administered through either peripheral or central venous access. If ECG changes persist after the initial dose, calcium administration should be repeated after 5 minutes. Patients receiving calcium therapy must be continuously monitored on a cardiac monitor to detect any potential arrhythmias or other complications. Calcium administration can increase the risk of digoxin toxicity, so caution is advised in patients on digoxin therapy. The effects of calcium are transient, so it is essential to combine calcium therapy with other treatments that have a longer duration of action to address hyperkalemia effectively.
